$comment: Rate conformance cases for ruling R16. These exist ONLY because of binary floating point, and they are shared rather than TypeScript-only because the Kotlin engine at AN2 shares the defect and must share the guard.
contract: BOTH the TypeScript engine and the Kotlin engine MUST consume this file. A divergence on any case fails both builds (D20). Never edit an expected value to make code pass: a case that will not pass is a question for the operator, never a code change.
rule: declarableRate = floor(numerator * 1e4 / denominator) / 1e2, computed on the INTEGRAL numerator and denominator - never on a pre-computed percentage. Truncation rounds toward zero, so the error is biased downward and never cancels, on the number filed with the AFC.
whyNormalisationIsNotEnough: The 1e6-style normalisation that fixes the proration in denominator-cases.json is useless here. 18.4 has no exact IEEE 754 representation, so normalising ~18.4 and then multiplying by 1e2 to reach hundredths reintroduces the same error. Only integer arithmetic works.
scan: Found by comparing the float form against exact integer arithmetic for every numerator against every denominator from 1 to 500: 72 disagreements in 125750 pairs. Every one has a denominator that is a multiple of 125, because n/125 lands on an exact tenth of a percent and exact tenths are the values binary cannot hold.
reachability: Denominator 125 is reachable on the simplified basis at employmentRate 52. Denominators 250, 375 and 500 are reachable only through the exact method, where an employer supplies the annual total directly - which is precisely the path that already carries EXACT_METHOD_UNVERIFIED.

floatFormRecorded: The floatFormWouldGive field records the MULTIPLY-FIRST float form, (numerator * 1e2) / denominator then truncated. That is the better naive attempt - it is what ruling R10 prescribes for the proration - and it is still wrong in these 72 cases. The more natural divide-first form, (numerator / denominator) * 1e2, is wrong in 172 of the same 125750 pairs. The lesson is that no float form is safe, not that one of them is.
